## Revenue forecasters' woes

- We don't truly know the present -- substantial data lags
- The past isn't what it used to be -- data revisions
- The economy we measure is not quite the economy we tax
- Must forecast *when* people pay, in addition to *what* they owe

Each issue adds to forecast risk. Each arises in slides below.

::: notes
Econ forecasters face the first 2 issues. But revenue forecasters face them and the next 2 as well.
Lags - PIT data from tax returns -- 2023 is latest full file
Data revisions -- employment data
Economy we tax -- capital gains
When people pay -- estimated tax and final returns
:::

# Population and employment

<!-- ## <span style="font-size: 0.8em;">Population change since the 2020 Census</span> -->

## Population change since the 2020 Census

```{r}
#| label: pop-change-facets
#| output: true
#| fig-width: 18
#| fig-height: 10

keep <- c(
  "npopchg",
  "naturalchg",
  "domesticmig",
  "internationalmig"
)
labels <- c(
  "Net Population Change",
  "Natural Change (Births minus Deaths)",
  "Domestic Migration",
  "International Migration"
)

pop |>
  filter(variable %in% keep) |>
  filter(year > 2020) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = keep, labels = labels)) |>
  arrange(variable) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = value, fill = variable)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Net Population Change" = "steelblue",
      "Natural Change (Births minus Deaths)" = "seagreen",
      "Domestic Migration" = "coral",
      "International Migration" = "mediumpurple"
    )
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  scale_x_discrete(name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "change (thousands)",
    labels = scales::label_comma(scale = 1e-3, accuracy = 1),
    limits = c(-350e3, 350e3),
    breaks = seq(-400e3, 400e3, 100e3)
  ) +
  ggtitle("Annual Changes in New York State Population Since 2020 Census") +
  labs(
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates Program\nChanges are from July 1 to July 1"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 2, scales = "fixed") +
  theme_presentation() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(size = rel(1.3), face = "bold")
  )

```

::: notes
These data are not lagged much, but they are highly uncertain. Analysts have had great difficulty reconciling the 2020 decennial census with previous annual population estimates.
:::

## [Downward NYS employment revisions ahead?]{style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

```{r}
#| label: employment-bench-nonbench-pchya

# compare NY Fed early benchmarked employment data to CES seasonally adjusted data

cesbase <- cesny |>
  filter(area_code == "00000", supersector_code == "00", seasonal == "S") |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(src = "ces") |>
  select(date, src, value)

ebenchbase <- ebench |>
  filter(area == "ny") |>
  mutate(src = "ebench") |>
  select(date, src, value = emp)

pdata <- bind_rows(cesbase, ebenchbase) |>
  filter(year(date) >= 2000) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(pchya = value / lag(value, 12) - 1, .by = src)

```

```{r}
#| label: show-employment-benchmark
#| output: true
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-retina: 2

# # | fig-width: 17.8
# # | fig-height: 10

emp_colors <- c(
  ces = "steelblue",
  ebench = "coral"
)

emp_labels <- c(
  ces = "Official employment (CES)",
  ebench = "Early benchmark (NY Fed)"
)

p <- pdata |>
  filter(year(date) >= 2022) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, pchya, colour = src)) +
  geom_line() + # linewidth = 1
  geom_point() + # size = 1
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", color = "blue") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = emp_colors, labels = emp_labels, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "% change",
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    breaks = seq(-0.1, 0.2, 0.01),
    minor_breaks = seq(-0.01, 0.20, 0.005), # minor ticks every 0.5%
    limits = c(-0.005, NA)
  ) +
  ggtitle("NYS employment % change vs. year ago") +
  scale_x_date(
    name = NULL,
    breaks = seq(as.Date("2022-01-01"), as.Date("2026-01-01"), by = "3 months"),
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(NA_Date_, as.Date("2025-12-10"))) +
  labs(
    caption = "Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics (CES) and New York Federal Reserve Bank (early benchmark)"
  ) +
  theme_presentation() +
  theme_rotate(angle = 45) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_line(color = "gray85", linewidth = 0.3)
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.position = c(0.85, 0.85),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.key.size = unit(1.5, "lines")
  )


# bounds (Dates)
xmin <- as.Date("2025-03-15")
xmax <- as.Date("2026-01-15")
ymin <- -0.005
ymax <- 0.02

# ellipse params in numeric-date units (days)
x0_n <- (as.numeric(xmin) + as.numeric(xmax)) / 2
a <- (as.numeric(xmax) - as.numeric(xmin)) / 2
y0 <- (ymin + ymax) / 2
b <- (ymax - ymin) / 2

# lots of points + explicit closure
n_pts <- 2000
t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n_pts)

ell_pts <- tibble(
  date = as.Date(x0_n + a * cos(t), origin = "1970-01-01"),
  pchya = y0 + b * sin(t)
)

# force closure by appending the first point
ell_pts <- dplyr::bind_rows(ell_pts, ell_pts[1, ])

p +
  geom_path(
    data = ell_pts,
    aes(x = date, y = pchya),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = "darkgreen",
    linetype = "solid",
    linewidth = 0.9,
    lineend = "round"
  )

```

::: notes
Initial employment data are based on relatively small sample of employers. U.S. BLS benchmarks these data annually to more comprehensive data from quarterly unemployment insurance tax records. NY Fed essentially mimics that process, but more frequently and sooner. DOB also does something similar, but not as frequenty.
:::

# Wages and withholding

## Wages

```{r}
#| label: wage=prep

tmp <- count(qcew, naics_level, naics, naics_title)

wages <- qcew |>
  filter(areatype == "state") |>
  filter(naics == "00" | str_starts(naics, "523")) |>
  select(-c(areatype, area, estab, contains("emp")))

wages2 <- wages |>
  mutate(
    ind = case_when(
      naics == "00" ~ "total",
      naics == "523" ~ "finance",
      naics == "5231" ~ "securities",
      naics == "5232" ~ "exchanges",
      naics == "5239" ~ "other",
      .default = "ERROR"
    )
  ) |>
  select(date, ind, totwage) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ind, values_from = totwage)

wages2 |>
  mutate(
    finshare = finance / total,
    across(c(finance, securities, exchanges, other), \(x) x / finance)
  )

wages3 <- wages2 |> select(date, total, finance)

```

```{r}
#| label: wages-plot
#| output: true

pdata <- wages3 |>
  rename(value = finance) |>
  filter(year(date) >= 2022) |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date) |> as.integer(),
    qtr = factor(
      paste0("Q", lubridate::quarter(date)),
      levels = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4")
    )
  )

yr_min <- min(pdata$year)
yr_max <- max(pdata$year)

facet_means <- pdata |>
  summarise(mean_value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .by = qtr)

pdata |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(
    data = facet_means,
    aes(yintercept = mean_value),
    color = "red",
    linetype = "solid",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~qtr, nrow = 1, scales = "fixed") + # one row, same y-axis across months
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(yr_min, yr_max, by = 1),
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.4, 0.4)) # add internal left/right padding
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::dollar_format(scale = 1e-9, suffix = "", accuracy = 0.1),
    breaks = seq(0, 100e9, by = 10e9),
    # limits = c(0, NA)
  ) +
  theme_presentation() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.8)),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(),
  ) +
  theme_rotate(angle = 90) +
  ggtitle(
    "QCEW Financial Sector (NAICS 523) Wages by Quarter, Calendar years 2023-2025",
    subtitle = "Red horizontal line is quarterly mean"
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "$ billions",
    x = NULL,
    caption = "Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics via NYS Department of Labor<br>**CAUTION: Vertical axis does not start at zero**"
  )

```

# Linking economic and tax-revenue forecasts

```{r}
#| label: get-agi-pi-data

# nysagi
# nyspi

agi2 <- nysagi |>
  filter(
    rstat == "All Filers",
    por == "All Places",
    county == "All Places",
    state == "All",
    country == "All"
  ) |>
  select(year, sortincome, agirange, numret:nyidadjust) |>
  arrange(sortincome, year)

agibase <- agi2 |>
  filter(sortincome == 16) |>
  select(year, nysagi) |>
  mutate(variable = "nysagi", value = nysagi) |>
  select(variable, year, value)

# agi2 |> filter(sortincome == 16) |> ggplot(aes(year, nysagi)) + geom_line()

pibase <- nyspi |>
  filter(linecode == 10, year %in% 2015:2023) |>
  mutate(
    variable = "nyspi",
    year = as.integer(year),
    value = as.numeric(value) * 1e6
  ) |>
  select(variable, year, value)

piagi <- bind_rows(pibase, agibase)

# piagi |> ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = variable)) + geom_line()
# piagi |>
#   pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value) |>
#   mutate(ratio = nyspi / nysagi) |>
#   ggplot(aes(year, ratio)) +
#   geom_line()
# pi is about 30-50% larger than agi depending on year

pdata <- piagi |>
  arrange(variable, year) |>
  mutate(pchya = value / lag(value) - 1, .by = variable) |>
  filter(year %in% 2016:2023)

```

## AGI vs. Personal Income Components

```{r}
#| label: get-agi-components

# nysagi
# nyspi
# wages, interest, dividends, capgains, caploss, rrpetgain, rrpetloss, busfarmgain, bus

agi_components <- nysagi |>
  filter(
    rstat == "All Filers",
    por == "All Places",
    county == "All Places",
    state == "All",
    country == "All"
  ) |>
  filter(sortincome == 16) |>
  select(
    year,
    numret,
    nysagi,
    wages,
    interest,
    dividends,
    capgains,
    caploss,
    rrpetgain,
    rrpetloss,
    busfarmgain,
    busfarmloss,
    pensions,
    otherinc
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

agibase <- agi_components |>
  mutate(
    intdiv = interest + dividends,
    capnet = capgains - caploss,
    rrpetnet = rrpetgain - rrpetloss,
    busfarmnet = busfarmgain - busfarmloss,
    allother = nysagi -
      wages -
      intdiv -
      capnet -
      rrpetnet -
      busfarmnet -
      pensions -
      otherinc
  ) |>
  select(
    year,
    nysagi,
    wages,
    intdiv,
    capnet,
    rrpetnet,
    busfarmnet,
    pensions,
    otherinc,
    allother
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

agibase2 <- agibase |>
  mutate(other = nysagi - wages - capnet) |>
  select(year, nysagi, wages, capnet, other)

# combine agi components plus nyspi
piagi <- agibase2 |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -year, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  bind_rows(pibase)

```

#| label: show-pi-agi-components

  scale_x_continuous(name = NULL, breaks = 2015:2024) +
  ggtitle("Growth Rates of Personal Income, AGI, and Major Components") +

    legend.title = element_blank(),

    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.key.size = unit(1.5, "lines")
  )

# Capital gains

## Why capital gains are important

::: {style="font-size: 0.65em;"}
- Large - about 10-18% of adjusted gross income, depending on year [@nysbudget2026ero]. Big impact on revenue
- Volatile - range greatly from year to year
- Concentrated - top 1.5% of taxpayers account for about 75% of capital gains realizations [@nys_pit_summary2]
- Hot money - can be shifted relatively easily across years by timing decisions of a small number of high-income taxpayers
- Payments on gains are volatile, too -- typically paid with quarterly estimated tax, especially January, and in the next fiscl year with April tax returns and extension requests
- Not included in traditional economic data - NIPA personal income excludes capital gains, whether realized or accrued [@bea_nipa_handbook_ch2]
:::

## Capital gains are concentrated

```{r}
#| label: capital-gains-shares-data

df <- nysagi |>
  filter(
    rstat == "All Filers",
    por == "All Places",
    county == "All Places",
    state == "All",
    country == "All",
    year == 2023
  ) |>
  # filter(sortincome == 16) |>
  select(year, sortincome, agirange, numret, nysagi, capgains) |>
  arrange(sortincome)

# df |>
#   mutate(across(c(numret, nysagi, capgains), \(x) x / x[sortincome == 16]))

# check totals
# df |>
#   mutate(group = ifelse(sortincome == 16, "total", "other")) |>
#   summarise(
#     across(c(numret, nysagi, capgains), \(x) sum(x)),
#     .by = group
#   )
# good, we can drop the totals row

# collapse to smaller groups

ilevs <- 1:4
ilabs <- c(
  "<$100k",
  "$100k-$500k",
  "$500k-$1m",
  ">= $1m"
)

df2 <- df |>
  filter(sortincome != 16) |>
  mutate(
    igroup = case_when(
      sortincome <= 10 ~ 1,
      sortincome %in% 11:13 ~ 2,
      sortincome == 14 ~ 3,
      sortincome == 15 ~ 4,
      .default = 0
    ),
    ilabel = factor(igroup, levels = ilevs, labels = ilabs)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    across(c(numret, nysagi, capgains), \(x) sum(x)),
    .by = c(igroup, ilabel)
  )
# df2

shares <- df2 |>
  mutate(across(c(numret, nysagi, capgains), \(x) x / sum(x))) |>
  select(igroup, ilabel, numret, capgains)


```

shares |>

## Capital gains episodes (national)

<br>

:::: {style="font-size: 0.55em;"}
|  |  |  |
|------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Period** | **Capital gains % of GDP** | **Context** |
| 1996-2000 | **rose 95%** from 3.2% to 6.3% | Dot-com boom |
| 2000-2002 | **fell 61%** from 6.3% to 2.5% | Dot-com bust |
| 2002-2007 | **rose 160%** from 2.5% to 6.4% | Credit + housing boom |
| 2007-2009 | **fell 72%** from 6.4% to 1.8% | Housing bust + Great Recession |
| 2009-2021 | **rose 380%** from 1.8% to 8.7% | Post-Great-Recession bull market; pandemic-era surge |
| 2021-2023 | **fell 60%** from 8.7% to 3.5% | Inflation shock, Fed tightening, 2022 bear market |
| 2023-2025 | **rose 52%** from 3.5% to 5.3% (*estimated*) | AI / mega-cap rally + broad market strength |

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; color: gray; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Notes: Capital gains realizations tend to move with asset prices, but they're much more volatile and can be shifted across years by timing decisions (e.g., harvesting gains and losses, reacting to anticipated policy changes). Percent changes based on unrounded numbers.<br>Source: Analysis of net capital gains realizations data in @cbo2026outlook.
:::
::::

## What drives capital gains realizations?

:::: {style="font-size: 0.55em;"}

Gains *available* to be realized:

- Equity market activity
- Real estate market activity
- Overall economic growth
- State-specific factors such as dominant industries (e.g., private equity, venture capital, tourism)

*Choices* about whether and when to realize gains:

- Current federal, state, and local tax rates -- e.g., higher rates can encourage holding assets longer, or shifting portfolios more toward interest- and divident-paying assets
- Expected future tax rates can trigger anticipatory responses -- e.g., sell now to beat next year's higher rate!
- Other factors may include liquidity concerns, cash flow needs, and risk tolerance

Even _**if**_ underlying stock market forecasts are correct (!) capital gains models tend to have huge errors.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; color: gray; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
See @nysbudget2025methodology for a good discussion of the DOB capital gains forecasting model.
:::
::::
